Loathe
LOHTH
verb
From the Saxon lāþian, “to hate, to be hateful,” from lāþ, “hateful, odious”; hence to feel disgust at, to abhor, to turn from with nausea of soul. The AV also spells it lothe.

Biblical Definition

To loathe is to abhor with disgust — not cool dislike but the soul turning from a thing with nausea. Scripture uses the word two ways, and the difference between them is the difference between damnation and repentance. First, men loathe what God gives. In the wilderness the people spake against God and against Moses, “and our soul loatheth this light bread” (Num 21:5) — the manna, bread from heaven, corn of angels, rained daily upon ingratitude. Solomon explains the palate: “The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet” (Pro 27:7). Fulness is the enemy of relish, and a soul stuffed with the world will gag on grace. Second, and this is the mercy, men loathe themselves. Ezekiel is the prophet of it: “ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed” (Eze 20:43); and again, “shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations” (Eze 36:31). Mark where the word falls in that chapter: after the new heart and the new spirit, after the sprinkling of clean water. Self-loathing for sin is not the cause of God’s mercy but its fruit; the man who sees the clean water is the man who at last sees the filth. Job says it plainly in the dust: “I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). So the manna-loather perishes and the self-loather lives.

Webster 1828 Definition

To feel disgust at; to abhor; to turn from with nausea of body or of soul.

expand to see more

LOATHE, to feel disgust at; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to food or drink.

Also, to hate; to dislike greatly; to abhor.

From Saxon lāþian, from lāþ, “hateful, odious.”

Israel’s soul loathed the manna, the bread of heaven (Num 21:5).

Ezekiel foretells the penitent loathing himself in his own sight (Eze 36:31).

Key Scripture

Num 21:5 — "And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread."

Eze 20:43 — "And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed."

Eze 36:31 — "Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations."

Pro 27:7 — "The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet."

Modern Corruption

The age has abolished self-loathing as a category and calls the abolition healing; Scripture calls the loathing of sin the first honest sight a man ever has of himself.

expand to see more

The therapeutic creed of our day holds that a man’s central problem is a low view of himself, and that the cure is to raise it — to esteem, accept, and validate the self as it stands. On that creed Ezekiel’s promise reads as a curse: ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight. But the creed is false at its root, because it mistakes the disease. The sinner’s ruin is not that he thinks too little of himself; it is that he loves himself supremely and God not at all, and every counsel that feeds that love feeds the ruin. Scripture never asks a man to invent a bad opinion of himself; it asks him to receive a true one. The publican who would not lift his eyes went down to his house justified, and the Pharisee who esteemed himself well went home condemned (Luk 18:13–14). What the age calls a wound is, in Ezekiel, the sign that the new heart has been given.

Yet the doctrine cuts the other way too, and the corruption has a second face: a brooding, unbelieving self-hatred that never comes to Christ, that gnaws at itself and calls the gnawing repentance. That is not Ezekiel’s loathing either, for his stands in a chapter of clean water, new heart, and a new spirit — the loathing of a pardoned man looking back. Godly sorrow works repentance unto salvation, not to be repented of; the sorrow of the world worketh death (2Co 7:10). And the deepest cure of the false appetite is the true one: the full soul loathes the honeycomb, so the LORD empties His people that manna may taste like manna again. Hunger for Christ is the end of loathing Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

To abhor with disgust — of the manna by the ungrateful, and of self by the penitent.

expand to see more

Loathe — Saxon lāþian, “to hate,” from lāþ, “odious.”

AV also spells the verb lothe (Eze 20:43; 36:31).

Israel loathed the manna — ingratitude gagging on grace (Num 21:5).

Fulness breeds loathing; hunger makes bitter things sweet (Pro 27:7).

Evangelical self-loathing follows the new heart; it does not purchase it.

Usage

"Our soul loatheth this light bread: the murmurer’s verdict on bread from heaven."

"Ezekiel’s penitent loathes himself after the clean water, not before it."

"The full soul loathes the honeycomb — a warning to every well-fed church."
